note: Add a pattern only when a blind test, a buyer report or the same choice across unrelated brands shows it. Each pattern is a default to avoid unless the brand or the brief chooses it on purpose.

patterns.description: Centred hero, then 3 benefit cards, then "How it works in 3 steps", then testimonials, then FAQ, then a final call to action, whatever the category.
patterns.why: It is the most common SaaS landing-page template in the model's training data, so it is what the model writes when nothing else decides the order.
patterns.fine_when: A new software product with no site yet, where the buyer's questions really come in that order and a real reference page uses it.
patterns.check: Compare the section kinds with the brand's own section order in brand-dna.json. If the candidate matches this stack and the brand's pages do not, flag it.

patterns.description: Purple, indigo or blue-to-violet gradients on the hero, buttons or section backgrounds.
patterns.why: Indigo was a framework default for years and models converge on it when no brand colour is given.
patterns.fine_when: The brand's measured palette already uses those colours or a gradient.
patterns.check: Any gradient, or any colour covering 3% or more of the page, that is not in the brand palette.

patterns.description: Inter, Geist, Poppins, Manrope, Space Grotesk or system-ui used in place of the brand's fonts.
patterns.why: These are the model's favourite modern sans fonts. A 'self-contained' or 'no external requests' brief also pushes it to system fonts without saying so.
patterns.fine_when: The brand uses that font, or it is a new brand and the font was chosen in the taste brief for a stated reason.
patterns.check: Font family per role (h1, h2, body, button, nav) against brand-dna.json, and whether the brand font file actually loaded.

patterns.description: Fully rounded pill buttons where the brand's buttons are square or barely rounded.
patterns.why: Pills read as friendly and modern, so the model picks them when the radius was not captured.
patterns.fine_when: The brand's buttons are pills (Allbirds' measured button radius is fully round).
patterns.check: Primary button radius against the brand's primary button radius.

patterns.description: Sentence-case, bold, 10 to 12 px rounded buttons replacing the brand's own button grammar, such as UPPERCASE letter-spaced labels.
patterns.why: Button case and letter spacing are rarely written in a brand brief, so the model's habit fills the gap.
patterns.fine_when: The brand's buttons are sentence case.
patterns.check: text-transform and letter-spacing of the primary button against the capture.

patterns.description: Rounded cards with soft shadows around every group of content.
patterns.why: Cards are the model's default way to group anything, and soft shadows read as polish.
patterns.fine_when: The brand's own components are rounded cards with shadows.
patterns.check: Card radius and shadows against shape.card_radius and shape.shadows in the capture.

patterns.description: Emoji used as feature icons or bullet markers.
patterns.why: Emoji are the cheapest icon the model can produce without assets.
patterns.fine_when: The brand uses emoji in its own site or social voice.
patterns.check: Emoji characters in headings, list items or icon slots.

patterns.description: Frosted-glass cards (blur, translucent white, thin light border) over a gradient.
patterns.why: A trend that is heavily over-represented in recent UI examples.
patterns.fine_when: The brand's product UI uses it and the page is about that product.
patterns.check: backdrop-filter blur or translucent white surfaces not in the capture.

patterns.description: A "Trusted by" or "As seen in" row with grey placeholder logos, invented names or logos the client never supplied.
patterns.why: The template expects social proof there, so the model fills the slot.
patterns.fine_when: Never with invented logos. Real logos with permission are fine.
patterns.check: Logo rows whose names are not in the client's facts or proof list.

patterns.description: A generic stock-style or generated hero image (laptop on desk, smiling team, abstract 3D shapes) instead of the real product or the brand's house photography.
patterns.why: It is what the model can make without the client's photos.
patterns.fine_when: The brand has no product photos yet and the image is labelled as a planned shot, not shipped.
patterns.check: Hero image source: is it one of the brand's images or in the house style seen in the screenshots?

patterns.description: Every section the same height, padding and layout rhythm.
patterns.why: One spacing rule applied everywhere is the simplest system to generate.
patterns.fine_when: The brand's pages really are that even.
patterns.check: Spread of section height_share in the candidate against the brand's sections.

patterns.description: The same fade-up entrance animation on every block.
patterns.why: One animation library call applied to every section is an easy way to look 'designed'.
patterns.fine_when: The brand's site animates that way, or one planned entrance on the first screen.
patterns.check: Count of elements with the same entrance animation class or keyframes.

patterns.description: The client's header and footer replaced by a minimal logo bar and a thin footer with a few links.
patterns.why: Landing-page templates strip navigation to 'focus' the visitor, and the model treats the page as standalone.
patterns.fine_when: A paid-traffic page where the client chose to remove navigation, recorded in DECISIONS.md, with the footer's legal and contact links kept.
patterns.check: Nav and footer item overlap with the capture (brand-fidelity-check, chrome).

patterns.description: Cream, ivory or beige backgrounds swapped in to look 'premium', 'artisan' or 'luxury'.
patterns.why: The model's idea of premium for jewellery, food, wellness and craft. In the Gehna test, one page put 30% of its area in cream against 2.9% on the live site.
patterns.fine_when: Cream is a measured brand surface at a similar share.
patterns.check: Area share of near-cream colours against the brand's share.

patterns.description: A minor brand colour (a badge or seasonal accent) promoted to the top bar, the main button or whole bands.
patterns.why: Colour lists without area shares make every colour look equal, and the model picks the 'prettier', higher-contrast one. In the Gehna test, wine went from about 1% to the top bar and the main button.
patterns.fine_when: The client asked for it for a campaign and it is in the change list.
patterns.check: palette area-share drift: an accent growing past twice its measured share.

patterns.description: An invented 'memorable' signature element (a custom price tag, a novel card shape, a decorative motif) that is not in the brand's component set.
patterns.why: Design skills tell the model to give every page one memorable thing, which is right for a new brand and wrong for an existing one.
patterns.fine_when: Mode is new, or the element is built only from the brand's tokens and the plan says why no existing component fits.
patterns.check: Components on the candidate with no match in the captured page (shape, colour, type).

patterns.description: Far fewer images and product modules than the brand's pages, with more white space.
patterns.why: The model's taste favours calm, sparse pages. Dense merchandising looks 'cluttered' to it even when buyers expect it.
patterns.fine_when: A deliberate test of a simpler page, recorded with its hypothesis.
patterns.check: images.per_1000px and image area share against the capture.

patterns.description: Every heading and paragraph centred.
patterns.why: Centring is the template's default for short marketing text.
patterns.fine_when: The brand centres its own sections.
patterns.check: text-align of section headings and body against the brand's pages.

patterns.description: Placeholder chips, dashed boxes, 'to shoot' image slots or 'client to supply' labels inside the page meant for launch.
patterns.why: The model is honest about gaps but puts them in the page instead of in a hand-off list.
patterns.fine_when: A review build that is clearly marked, with a clean launch build beside it.
patterns.check: brand-fidelity-check, placeholders.

patterns.description: Sale prices, countdowns and dated offers written straight into the markup.
patterns.why: The model copies what it saw on the day. In the Gehna test the sale price went stale within a day.
patterns.fine_when: The offer is held in one dated data block with an end date.
patterns.check: Prices and offers against the capture date (brand-fidelity-check, facts).

patterns.description: A bento grid of mismatched tiles for features.
patterns.why: A recent trend in product marketing pages that models now reach for.
patterns.fine_when: The brand's site uses it.
patterns.check: Grid sections with tiles of 3 or more different sizes not in the capture.

patterns.description: Unlock, elevate, seamless, game-changer, supercharge, effortless, empower, transform, revolutionise, delve, harness.
patterns.why: These words appear far more often in model output than in human writing about the same subjects.
patterns.fine_when: The word is in the client's own voice samples.
patterns.check: Search the text for the list and compare with voice.samples.

patterns.description: "In today's fast-paced world", "Ever wondered", "Tired of", "Say goodbye to", "Meet X".
patterns.why: Stock openers are the most likely first words for a marketing paragraph.
patterns.fine_when: Almost never. Start with the specific thing.
patterns.check: The first five words of each section.

patterns.description: Lists of exactly three everywhere: three benefits, three adjectives, three steps.
patterns.why: Three reads as complete and rhythmic, so the model uses it by reflex.
patterns.fine_when: There really are three things.
patterns.check: Count lists and adjective triplets; more than two on one page is a flag.

patterns.description: Formula headlines: "The smarter way to X", "X, without the Y", "It's not X. It's Y.", "Not just X. Y."
patterns.why: These shapes score well in copywriting examples, so they are the model's default headline.
patterns.fine_when: The client's best-performing ads use that shape, with evidence.
patterns.check: Headline shape against the client's own headlines in voice.samples.

patterns.description: "Limited time", "Only a few left", countdowns and "Don't miss out" with no real deadline or stock count.
patterns.why: Urgency is a standard conversion device in templates.
patterns.fine_when: A real, dated offer or a real stock figure from the capture.
patterns.check: Each urgency claim traced to a fact with a date.

patterns.description: Benefits any competitor could claim: high quality, great service, fast shipping, made with love.
patterns.why: With no specific facts, the model writes the category average.
patterns.fine_when: Never as the main claim. Replace with the specific fact ("BIS hallmarked", "7-day return and exchange").
patterns.check: Could a competitor publish this sentence unchanged? If yes, flag it.

patterns.description: "Trusted by thousands", "Loved by 10,000+ customers", star ratings or quotes not in the facts.
patterns.why: Templates have a proof slot and the model fills it with plausible numbers.
patterns.fine_when: Never. Use captured numbers with their source and date.
patterns.check: Every number traced to facts in brand-dna.json or a supplied source.

patterns.description: A consultant-style explanatory voice replacing the brand's own register (short and plain, ornate, playful, technical).
patterns.why: The model's helpful-assistant voice is its average register.
patterns.fine_when: The brand has no voice yet and the taste brief chose one.
patterns.check: Sentence length, we/you ratio and word choice against voice.stats and voice.samples.

patterns.description: Every concept in a batch shares one look: the same layout, type treatment and colour block.
patterns.why: The model varies wording, not art direction, unless the axes are named.
patterns.fine_when: A deliberate test of copy only, with the look held constant on purpose.
patterns.check: Put the thumbnails side by side; if they differ only in words, flag it.

patterns.description: The same hook formula reused across variants: "POV:", "Stop scrolling", "3 reasons why", "I tried X so you don't have to".
patterns.why: Hook formulas from creator advice are heavily represented in training data.
patterns.fine_when: The client's own winning ads use the formula, with results.
patterns.check: First line of each variant; repeated structure across more than one in five is a flag.

patterns.description: The product cut out and floated on a soft gradient or a plain studio colour.
patterns.why: It is the easiest product image to generate and needs no scene.
patterns.fine_when: The brand's own ads use that look.
patterns.check: Background of each product image against the brand's house photo style.

patterns.description: Variants that differ only in colour, crop or wording instead of in idea, proof, offer or audience.
patterns.why: Surface variation is cheap and looks like range.
patterns.fine_when: A planned creative test of one surface variable.
patterns.check: Name the axis each variant changes. If every axis is colour, crop or wording, flag the batch.

patterns.description: A fixed checklist score out of 100 with no diagnosis of why this account's or page's numbers moved.
patterns.why: Checklists are easy to complete without understanding the business.
patterns.fine_when: As a short hygiene pass after the specific diagnosis.
patterns.check: Does the top finding name a number from this account or page and a cause specific to it?

patterns.description: An audit that ends in 'rebuild the page' when its findings are each fixable on the live page.
patterns.why: A new design feels like a bigger answer, and the model enjoys building.
patterns.fine_when: The brand or business changed, the page hit a ceiling after tested patches, or traffic is too low to test.
patterns.check: Each finding mapped to one change on the live page, with evidence and a test.

patterns.description: "Add social proof", "Improve your call to action", "Make it mobile friendly" with no evidence from this page.
patterns.why: Best-practice lists are the average answer to 'audit my page'.
patterns.fine_when: Never without a screenshot, a number or a quote from this page.
patterns.check: Each recommendation cites what was seen, where, and at which screen size.

patterns.description: A SWOT, 4P or three-option frame filled with statements that fit any business in the category.
patterns.why: Frameworks give structure without needing facts.
patterns.fine_when: The frame is filled with this business's numbers and named competitors.
patterns.check: Strike the business name. Could the plan belong to a competitor?

patterns.description: Three options where two are weak on purpose so the third wins.
patterns.why: The model has already chosen and builds options to justify it.
patterns.fine_when: Never. Each option should be one a sensible person might pick.
patterns.check: Write the strongest case for each losing option. If you cannot, the options are straw.
